title: The Effort and Efficacy Beliefs
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart treats Effort and Efficacy as intertwined third-layer beliefs in his Five Key Beliefs pyramid, connected through what he calls the Effort-Efficacy Flywheel. He distinguishes Effort unbelief in low-confidence students from Carol Dweck's false growth mindset in high-achieving students who mistake ability for something innate. He directly critiques popular misreadings of growth mindset, the false idea that it's a fixed trait one either has or doesn't, and the oversimplified maxim to always praise process over outcome regardless of whether the process actually worked. Three core strategies, Woodenization, Define Success, and Unpack Outcomes, are named as the interventions that target the flywheel's breakage points.
points: Stuart's Effort-Efficacy Flywheel model frames the two beliefs as mutually reinforcing, or breaking down into a doom loop if any link fails.
He identifies an overlooked group at risk of Effort unbelief, high-achieving students who credit innate ability rather than a trail of experiences of growth, which Dweck calls a false growth mindset.

His critique of popular growth-mindset culture targets treating it as a binary trait rather than a context-dependent spectrum, and blindly praising effort even when the effort produced a genuinely bad result.
Praising ineffective effort regardless of outcome, he argues, sends students the false signal that school is a bizarre place where outcomes don't matter.
quotes: The Effort belief is absent when you don't think you can improve.
But when a student thinks Effort is something detached from their ability to improve, make no mistake: that is a student inflicted with Effort unbelief.
It's hard to overstate how powerfully our beliefs about our Efficacy predict our performance.
You hear a lot of people saying, I'm a growth mindset person, but it turns out that we're all a mixture, often depending on the environment we're in.
Valorizing ineffective Effort sends a signal to students that school is a bizarre place where outcomes don't matter—all that matters is that you try.
All human beings want to be motivated. This student does, too. There's just something getting in the way right now—something that you get to work at puzzling out.
